title: Network Policies
summary: Restrict Pod traffic at L3/L4 with podSelector, namespaceSelector and ipBlock rules, default-deny policies and a supporting network plugin.

blocks.text: Out of the box, any bay can phone any other bay. **Fences and gate passes** (NetworkPolicy) change that, controlling who may connect by address and port (layer 3 or 4). Passes name allowed bays, company yards (namespaces) or address ranges (IP blocks). A bay can always reach itself, and its own ship can always reach it. But the fences only exist if the road contractor (network plugin) knows how to build them.
A NetworkPolicy controls traffic at the **IP address or port level (OSI layer 3 or 4)** for TCP, UDP and SCTP. It applies to connections that have a selected Pod on one or both ends.

steps.text: By default Pods are non-isolated: they accept traffic from any source.
Once a **NetworkPolicy** selects the `db` Pod for ingress, only traffic the policy allows can reach it.
This policy allows the frontend Pods, so their traffic gets through.
Traffic from other Pods is dropped. Enforcement needs a network plugin that supports NetworkPolicy.

blocks.text: The **network plugin** enforces policies. Without a networking solution that supports NetworkPolicy, creating the object **has no effect**.
Allowed peers are identified by three things:

items: **Pods** (a Pod can never block access to itself).
**Namespaces**.
**IP blocks** (CIDR ranges). Traffic to and from the Pod's own node is always allowed.

blocks.text: A bay with no policy is open both ways. Once any policy selects it for incoming traffic, it is **fenced in**: only listed callers get through, plus its own ship, and replies to allowed calls flow automatically. Outgoing works the same way. There are no "keep out" signs, only passes, and passes simply add up, so order never matters. For bay A to reach bay B, A's outgoing pass and B's incoming pass must both allow it.

items: By default a Pod is **non-isolated** for both ingress and egress: all connections are allowed.
A Pod becomes **isolated for ingress** once any NetworkPolicy selects it and has `Ingress` in `policyTypes`. Egress works the same way with `Egress`.
An isolated Pod only allows what some applicable policy's rules allow (plus, for ingress, connections from its own node). **Reply traffic** for allowed connections is allowed implicitly.
Policies are **additive** and never conflict: the result is the union of all applicable policies, so evaluation order doesn't matter.
Pod A to Pod B works only if **A's egress and B's ingress** both allow it.

blocks.text: There are no deny rules. The model is deny by default once isolated, then you add allow rules.

A policy form starts with which bays it guards (`podSelector`); an empty selector `{}` guards every bay in the yard. `policyTypes` says whether it fences incoming, outgoing or both. Each incoming rule lets a caller through only if both its origin (`from`) and door (`ports`) match; outgoing rules match `to` plus `ports`. A rule can open a run of doors with `endPort`, if the contractor supports it.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: <policy-name>
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      <key>: <value>       # Pods this policy applies to
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: <cidr>
        except:
        - <cidr>
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          <key>: <value>
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          <key>: <value>
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: <port>
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: <cidr>
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: <port>

items: `spec.podSelector` picks the Pods the policy applies to. An **empty** `podSelector: {}` selects **all Pods in the namespace**.
`policyTypes` can hold `Ingress`, `Egress` or both. If omitted, `Ingress` is always set, and `Egress` is set only if the policy has egress rules.
Each ingress rule allows traffic matching **both** its `from` and `ports`; each egress rule matches both `to` and `ports`.
A port range is possible with `endPort` (≥ `port`, needs `port`, both numeric). If the plugin doesn't support `endPort`, only `port` is applied.

sections.heading: from/to selectors: the AND vs OR trap

blocks.text: Passes can name callers several ways: tagged bays in this yard (`podSelector`), every bay in tagged yards (`namespaceSelector`), or address ranges (`ipBlock`) for visitors from outside the port. Combine yard and bay tags in **one** entry and both must match (AND). List them as **two** entries and either will do (OR). Yards are picked by tag, never by name, but every yard carries a fixed name tag `kubernetes.io/metadata.name`.

rows: Pods in the policy's own namespace
CIDR ranges (use for cluster-external IPs; Pod IPs are ephemeral)

blocks.text:
# ONE entry = AND: role=client Pods in namespaces labelled user=alice
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        user: alice
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        role: client

# TWO entries = OR: role=client Pods in this namespace, OR any Pod in user=alice namespaces
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        user: alice
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        role: client

items: Namespaces can't be named directly; select them by label. The control plane sets the immutable label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` (value = namespace name) on every namespace.
When unsure how a policy was read, run `kubectl describe` on it.
Whether IP rewriting (e.g. by a LoadBalancer or Service) happens before or after policy processing is undefined, so ipBlock results can vary by plugin.

blocks.text: With no policies, a yard is wide open. A common first move is a yard-wide fence: select every bay (`podSelector: {}`), list the directions, and add no rules, so nothing passes. Careful: fencing all outgoing calls also blocks calls to the port phone directory (DNS), so add a pass for that. An "allow everything" pass for one direction means no other policy can close it.
With no policies in a namespace, all ingress and egress is allowed. These namespace-wide policies all use `podSelector: {}`:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
A default-deny **egress** policy also blocks **DNS**. If workloads need name resolution, create an additional policy that permits egress to the cluster DNS service.
An allow-all policy means no other policy can deny that direction for those Pods. Each of these leaves the other direction's isolation unchanged.

sections.heading: Hands-on: restrict access to a Service

blocks.text: Try it in the yard. Start an `nginx` contract and phone it from a temporary `busybox` bay: it answers. Now post a pass saying only bays tagged `access=true` may call bays tagged `app=nginx`. The untagged busybox's call now times out. Start a new busybox with `--labels="access=true"` and it gets through. Plugins that can build these fences include Calico, Cilium, Antrea and Kube-router.
Plugins with NetworkPolicy support include Antrea, Calico, Cilium and Kube-router.

kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80
kubectl run busybox --rm -ti --image=busybox -- /bin/sh
# inside the Pod:
wget --spider --timeout=1 nginx      # works before any policy

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: access-nginx
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          access: "true"

items: The `app=nginx` label was added to the Pods automatically by `kubectl create deployment`.
After applying, `wget` from an unlabelled Pod **times out**.
A Pod started with `--labels="access=true"` gets through.

blocks.text: Fast test loop: `kubectl run busybox --rm -ti --labels="access=true" --image=busybox -- /bin/sh`, then `wget --spider --timeout=1 <service>`. Run it with and without the label to prove the policy works.

Fences have gaps. Full blocking is only promised for TCP, UDP and SCTP calls. Passes cover the whole bay, every container in it. A brand-new bay may start before its fence goes up, and whether calls already in progress get cut is up to the contractor. Bays wired straight into the ship (hostNetwork) are a grey area. And you cannot post "keep out" signs, fence port phone numbers by name, or log calls.

items: Deny-all is only guaranteed for TCP, UDP and SCTP. ICMP, ARP and other protocols are undefined. SCTP needs a CNI plugin that supports it.
Policies apply at Pod level, so they cover init, sidecar and regular containers alike.
A Pod created before the plugin handles a new policy may start unprotected. Allow rules may land after isolation rules.
Policy changes may or may not affect **existing connections**; it's implementation defined.
hostNetwork Pods: behaviour is undefined. Most plugins treat their traffic as node traffic.
Not possible with the API: explicit deny rules, TLS, targeting Services by name, node identities, cluster-wide default policies, logging, or blocking localhost and node traffic.

flashcards.front: What enforces NetworkPolicy, and what happens without it?
flashcards.back: The network plugin. Without a plugin that supports NetworkPolicy, the objects have no effect.

flashcards.front: Default isolation state of a Pod with no policies selecting it?
flashcards.back: Non-isolated for both ingress and egress: all traffic allowed.
All Pods in the policy's namespace.

flashcards.front: policyTypes is omitted. What gets set?
flashcards.back: Ingress always; Egress only if the policy has egress rules.

flashcards.front: Two policies select the same Pod with different allow rules. Result?
flashcards.back: The union of both. Policies are additive and never conflict.

flashcards.front: namespaceSelector and podSelector in ONE from entry vs TWO entries?
flashcards.back: One entry = AND (those Pods in those namespaces). Two entries = OR.

flashcards.front: Spec for a default deny-all-ingress policy?
flashcards.back: podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress], with no ingress rules.

flashcards.front: Side effect of a default deny-all egress policy?
flashcards.back: It blocks DNS too. Add a policy allowing egress to the cluster DNS service.

flashcards.front: How do you target one namespace by its name?
flashcards.back: Select the immutable label kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<namespace> in a namespaceSelector.
endPort ≥ port, port must also be set, both numeric. Unsupported plugins apply only port.

flashcards.front: Which traffic can a Pod never block with NetworkPolicy?
flashcards.back: Traffic to itself, and traffic to/from its own node.

questions.stem: You apply a valid NetworkPolicy, but traffic is unaffected. What's the most likely reason?

options.text: The cluster's network plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy
options.explanation: Policies are implemented by the network plugin; without support they do nothing.

options.text: NetworkPolicies only take effect after the namespace is recreated
options.explanation: No such step exists; the plugin applies policies as it handles them.
They can cover ingress, egress or both.

options.text: The policy needs an ipBlock to be valid
options.explanation: ipBlock is one of several optional peer types; it isn't required.

questions.stem: In a namespace with no NetworkPolicies, all ingress and egress traffic to and from its Pods is allowed.

options.explanation: Pods are non-isolated by default in both directions.
Isolation only starts once a policy selects the Pod.

questions.stem: A policy has a podSelector and an `egress` section but no `policyTypes`. Which types apply?

options.explanation: Ingress is always set; Egress is added because egress rules exist.
Ingress is always set when policyTypes is omitted.
Egress is also set when the policy has egress rules.
policyTypes is optional and has defaults.

questions.stem: An ingress `from` list has two entries: one with `namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {user: alice}}` and a separate one with `podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: client}}`. What is allowed?

options.text: role=client Pods in the local namespace, OR any Pod in namespaces labelled user=alice
options.explanation: Two separate entries are ORed.

options.text: Only role=client Pods inside namespaces labelled user=alice
options.explanation: That AND meaning needs both selectors in a single entry.
A podSelector alone selects Pods in the policy's own namespace.

options.text: Nothing, because mixing selectors is invalid
options.explanation: Mixing is valid; the YAML structure decides AND vs OR.

questions.stem: Which spec creates a default deny for all ingress in a namespace, leaving egress alone?

options.text: podSelector: {} with policyTypes: [Ingress] and no ingress rules
options.explanation: Selects every Pod and allows no ingress.
An empty rule {} allows all ingress.
That denies egress as well.
That denies egress, not ingress.

questions.stem: After adding a default deny-all egress policy, Pods can't resolve Service names. What fixes it while keeping the deny?

options.text: Add a separate NetworkPolicy allowing egress to the cluster's DNS service
options.explanation: The docs warn deny-all egress blocks DNS and say to allow DNS egress separately.
DNS lookups are outbound from the Pod; ingress rules don't help.

options.text: Add an ingress rule with an explicit deny for DNS
options.explanation: NetworkPolicy has no deny rules, and the problem is egress.

options.text: Nothing; DNS is always exempt from NetworkPolicy
options.explanation: It isn't: deny-all egress also blocks DNS.

questions.stem: Which statements about combining NetworkPolicies are correct? Select 2.

options.text: Allowed connections are the union of all policies that apply to the Pod
options.explanation: Policies are additive.

options.text: For Pod A to reach Pod B, A's egress and B's ingress must both allow it
options.explanation: If either side doesn't allow it, the connection doesn't happen.

options.text: A later policy can deny what an earlier one allowed
options.explanation: There are no deny rules and order doesn't matter.

options.text: Reply traffic must be allowed by an explicit rule
options.explanation: Replies to allowed connections are allowed implicitly.

questions.stem: You need to allow traffic from a namespace called `monitoring`, which has no custom labels. What should you select?

options.explanation: The control plane sets this immutable label to the namespace name on every namespace.

options.text: A namespace: monitoring field inside the from entry
options.explanation: Namespaces can't be named directly; a label selector is required.

options.text: An ipBlock with the namespace's CIDR
options.explanation: Namespaces have no CIDR; ipBlock is meant for cluster-external IPs.
That label is on namespaces, and podSelector alone only looks in the policy's namespace.

questions.stem: With an ingress policy applied, a Pod can block connections from the node it runs on.

options.explanation: Traffic from the Pod's node is always allowed.
Correct: blocking node or localhost traffic isn't possible with the API.

questions.stem: An egress rule uses `port: 32000` and `endPort: 32768` with protocol TCP. What does it allow?

options.text: TCP to any port from 32000 to 32768 at the matching destinations
options.explanation: endPort turns port into the start of a range.
It is a range, not two ports.
Rules only allow; there's no exclusion for ports.

options.text: It's invalid because endPort needs a named port
options.explanation: Both port and endPort must be numeric.

questions.stem: Which can NOT be done with the NetworkPolicy API? Select 3.

options.text: Target a Service by its name
options.explanation: Listed as unsupported; target Pods or namespaces by label instead.
The API only has allow rules.
Logging security events is listed as unsupported.

options.text: Allow ingress only from a CIDR range
options.explanation: ipBlock does exactly this.

questions.stem: Policy `access-nginx` selects `app: nginx` and allows ingress only from Pods labelled `access: "true"`. Which test Pod reaches the nginx Service?

options.explanation: The labelled Pod matches the from podSelector, so wget succeeds.
Without the label, the walkthrough shows wget timing out.
This creates the Service; it doesn't start a client Pod.

questions.stem: Which of these is listed as a network provider with NetworkPolicy support?

options.explanation: Calico is listed with Antrea, Cilium and Kube-router.
busybox is the test client image in the walkthrough.
nginx is the sample workload being protected.

questions.stem: A deny-all policy is in place. What is guaranteed about ICMP (ping) traffic?

options.text: Nothing; behaviour for ICMP is undefined and varies by plugin
options.explanation: Deny is only guaranteed for TCP, UDP and SCTP.
Some plugins may allow it.
Some plugins may deny it.
